title: Mandodari
hook: Ravana's queen walks onto the battlefield, and says what no one else could say

segments.voice: Yesterday: Aditya Hridayam, a hymn to the sun, and one arrow, heads that grew back, and the weapon of Brahma. Did you step into the light when you were tired? Today, the war is over, and someone comes out of the city to grieve. Day six hundred fifty-six.

When the noise of victory dies down, the gates of Lanka open, and the women of Ravana's palace come out onto the battlefield. They've lost husbands, sons, brothers. They walk among the dead, weeping, until they find him. And one of them comes forward to the body and kneels. She is Mandodari, Ravana's chief queen, Indrajit's mother. She has lost her son, and now her husband. Valmiki lets her speak over him at length.
screen: `THE GATES OPEN.` → `THE WOMEN COME OUT.` → `MANDODARI KNEELS.`

segments.voice: Her lament holds love and truth at the same time. She remembers who he was. You frightened the gods, she says. Indra himself feared you. The earth and the mountains trembled at your name. How could a man on foot, wandering in the forest, bring you down? And then she answers her own question, in two ways. First she says Rama can't be only a man. In Valmiki's words as she grieves, he must be the eternal, the supreme, Vishnu himself, come in human form. A queen of Lanka is the one who says it out loud, over her husband's body. Then she turns to Ravana's own part in it, gently and without flinching. Long ago, she says, you conquered your senses, and with that discipline you conquered the three worlds. Now, it's as if your senses remembered and took their revenge. Your desire for Sita did what no army could. She says she warned him. She says Sita's faithfulness was a fire he couldn't hold. And then she simply grieves: her husband, her son, her life in pieces. She falls across his chest and weeps. Later tradition honored her. A well-known Sanskrit verse names five women of the epics whose remembrance is said to wash away wrongdoing, and Mandodari is one of them. Valmiki's portrait suggests why. She's loyal without being blind. She sees her husband whole, the greatness and the ruin, and she mourns him anyway.
screen: `YOU FRIGHTENED THE GODS.` · `RAMA IS MORE THAN A MAN.` · `YOUR SENSES TOOK REVENGE.` · `ONE OF THE FIVE WOMEN.` · then, large: `LOYAL WITHOUT BEING BLIND.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath be soft. Think of someone you love who has real faults, maybe someone you've lost. Let yourself see them whole, as Mandodari did: what was great in them, and what went wrong. Don't argue with either. Hold both in the same breath. Breathe in with the love. Breathe out with the honesty. Let them sit together. The bell holds the time.
Mandodari. Ravana's chief queen and Indrajit's mother, who grieves him on the battlefield, naming both his greatness and the desire that destroyed him.
Your line: loyal without being blind. Today, remember one person whole, the good and the hard, with love. Day six hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Some Hindus recite a traditional verse naming five revered women of the epics, the pañcakanyā, with Mandodari among them, and some say it in the morning; versions differ on one of the names.

myth: Mandodari curses Rama over Ravana's body
she says Rama must be more than a man, and names Ravana's own fault.
she says Ravana once conquered his senses
and that his desire for Sita was their revenge.
she mourns him and names his fault in the same lament.

fork.setup: you're Mandodari, kneeling by Ravana's body after losing your son and husband. what do you say?
options: say only that he was great.
name his greatness and his fault, and grieve him anyway.
fork.reveal: she recalls his power, says Rama must be Vishnu, names Ravana's desire as his undoing, and weeps over him.

original.note: Sanskrit Mandodarī: Ravana's chief queen and Indrajit's mother, counted by tradition among the five revered women.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ravana's queen was a minor character.
what it means: she speaks over Ravana's whole life: his greatness, his fault, and her grief.
what a scholar hears: tradition counts her among the pañcakanyā, five revered women whose remembrance is said to wash away wrongdoing.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 110–111 (the women of Lanka come out; Mandodari's lament)
The pañcakanyā verse (ahalyā draupadī sītā tārā mandodarī tathā)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering; confirm.
Mandodari's identification of Rama as Vishnu, the eternal supreme self (often cited as vyaktam eṣa mahāyogī paramātmā sanātanaḥ): paraphrased; confirm.
The senses-taking-revenge image (indriyāṇi purā jitvā jitaṃ tribhuvanaṃ tvayā / smaradbhir iva tad vairam indriyair eva nirjitaḥ): paraphrased; confirm.
The pañcakanyā verse: versions vary (Sita or Kunti); the script says only that Mandodari is among the five.
The meaning of the name Mandodarī ('slender-waisted'): confirm.

Editor review (651–668 pass): cut the superlative 'one of the most remarkable speeches in the epic', the unsourced 'in a few short days', and 'the last word on Ravana's life' (Vibhishana also laments him); practice no longer tells the listener what they feel; the name etymology ('slender-waisted') was removed from the original game under the claims rule.
